tier_reason: Methodology alone would reach A (fannkuchredux/test.c and test.js public, gcc 12.2.0 with -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops in tools/languages.rb, nodejs 19.7.0, Ryzen 7 3800X), but the two programs use different algorithms and the same table shows a gcc -O3 build of the faster algorithm (Cython row, 0.13 s) beating Node (0.15 s), so the C baseline is algorithmically handicapped against a tuned JS program and the language-level claim falls under the crippled-baseline precedent (tier D).

corrections.workload: Benchmarks Game fannkuch-redux at n=10 (tools/benchmarks.rb args [10, TEST_COUNT], TEST_COUNT 5): one process runs the kernel 5 times and each run prints its own in-language time (C clock(), JS Date); Best T is the minimum of those in-process times, so start-up is excluded and JIT warm-up is largely excluded. Single thread.
corrections.claimed_speedup: fannkuchredux (README round 1, 2023-02-28): Node 0.15 s vs C 0.21 s best run (about 1.4x, derived from page data); GraalVM_JVM 0.18 s and GraalVM 0.19 s also below C; Lua JIT 0.27 s slower. Same table: Cython 0.13 s (Cython-generated C built with the same gcc flags, Pall-style flip loop) beats Node, and Crystal 0.19 s (same algorithm as the C program) roughly ties C.
corrections.caveats: Not the same algorithm: test.js is Isaac Gouy's transliteration of Mike Pall's Lua program (caches the first element, writes q[q0]=q0, skips the swap loop when q0 < 3, sign-swap permutation step), while test.c is the Oleg Mazurov Java-derived program (reverses the full prefix including element 0 on every flip, VLA arrays). The suite's own Cython program, a Pall-style variant compiled by gcc with the same -O3 flags, runs in 0.13 s and beats Node's 0.15 s, so the Node win over C is algorithmic, not a JIT effect; README's 'one algorithm' promise does not hold for this benchmark. Timing is in-language (C clock() CPU time, JS Date wall time), best of 5 runs inside one process at n=10, so the earlier note that start-up is included was wrong. Numbers date from 2023-02-28 (gcc 12.2.0, nodejs 19.7.0); the only commit since 2023-03-30 is a README link (2026-01-27). V8 is a known entry; this record is a language-level claim kept under the suite repo.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithm, not the JIT: the JS program uses Mike Pall's cheaper flip scheme while the C program reverses the whole prefix each flip; a gcc -O3 build of a Pall-style program (Cython row) is faster than Node in the same table.

notes: Numbers on the README match the record (Node 0.15 s, C 0.21 s, GraalVM 0.18/0.19 s, LuaJIT 0.27 s), but the record's workload was wrong (n=10 with 5 in-process runs and in-language timers, not n=7 with start-up included). Shortcoming to record: different algorithms; the suite's own Cython row (gcc -O3, Pall-style loop, 0.13 s) beats Node, so the C baseline is crippled for this comparison (tier D). last_commit 2026-01-27 is within 12 months, so status is active by rule, though code is unchanged since 2023-03-30.

tier_reason: The numbers (up to 2.8x AMD, 1.78x NVIDIA end-to-end vs AOT; 1.23x average over Jitify) come from the CGO 2025 paper and were seen only in WebSearch snippets of the CGO program page, LLNL newsroom and HPCwire (all unresolvable here), so the wave-14 rule keeps it at C; the public harness Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks (driver.py, hecbench.toml, per-benchmark Makefiles with aot/proteus/jitify builds) has no results, GPU models or CPU stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Public harness (Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks): AOT and Proteus variants of each HeCBench program are built from the same main.cu by the same Makefile with Clang (PROTEUS_CC), -std=c++14 -O3 -ffast-math, CUDA default --cuda-gpu-arch=sm_70; the Proteus build only adds -fpass-plugin=libProteusPass.so and -DENABLE_PROTEUS. The paper's exact compiler versions and flags were not read (paper blocked).
corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the CGO 2025 paper (Georgakoudis, Parasyris, Beckingsale, pp. 507-522, peer-reviewed, would be tier B if read), its CGO program page, the LLNL newsroom and HPCwire were all unresolvable from this environment, and the Proteus README and docs carry no numbers or paper link. 'Up to' maxima are best cases on selected applications; the public harness (Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks: HeCBench adam, feynman-kac, LULESH and others, plus RAJAPerf and LBANN configs) builds AOT and JIT variants with identical -O3 -ffast-math flags but publishes no results, and GPU models are not stated (the CUDA Makefile default sm_70 suggests a V100-class part, unconfirmed). End-to-end times include JIT compile overhead per the paper abstract snippet. The repo has moved: github.com/Olympus-HPC/proteus now resolves to llnl/proteus.

notes: Metadata checked: 54 stars, 10 forks, 397 commits, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, last commit 2026-10-09 (active). The repo URL now redirects to github.com/llnl/proteus (README clones LLNL/proteus; the Olympus-HPC org no longer lists it), so consider a repo_url override to https://github.com/llnl/proteus while keeping the merged id. Retier to B if the CGO 2025 paper becomes readable; harness code at github.com/Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks shows AOT and JIT builds use identical flags.

tier_reason: A for ipnsort: writeup/sort_safety/text.md states rustc 1.75.0-nightly, clang 16.0.6, gcc 13.2.1, Ryzen 9 5900X, links build.rs at commit 190b3ec (C++ opt_level(3), -std=c++20; Rust --release, lto=thin), the bench code (benches/, src/cpp/cpp_std_sort.cpp calling std::sort(data, data+len) with the default comparator for u64) is public, and the plot labels give per-pattern times. Claim narrowed: driftsort is not in this benchmark and the then-current Rust stable sort loses to the C++ stable sorts on several patterns.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Plot values in writeup/sort_safety/assets/unstable-hot-u64-10k.png (10k u64, hot, Zen 3, time in us): rust_ipnsort_unstable vs libstdc++ std::sort / libc++ std::sort: ascending 2.07 vs 49.3 / 6.23 (23.8x / 3.0x), descending 3.16 vs 32.2 / 11.4 (10.2x / 3.6x), random 77.0 vs 297.6 / 265.1 (3.9x / 3.4x), random_d20 24.3 vs 136.5 / 97.6 (5.6x / 4.0x), random_p5 12.4 vs 57.2 / 16.7 (4.6x / 1.35x), random_s95 83.4 vs 182.2 / 84.2 (2.2x / 1.01x), random_z1 56.8 vs 222.9 / 200.2 (3.9x / 3.5x) (ratios derived from page data). The text's 'current Rust standard library unstable sort ... outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts' refers to the pre-2024 pdqsort-based rust_std_unstable (random 136.9 us). Stable plot: driftsort is not tested; the then-current rust_std_stable beats libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random (253.0 vs 318.6 us) but loses on random_d20 (250.5 vs 190.5) and random_p5 (156.8 vs 69.8) and loses to libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1.
corrections.workload: Sorting 10k u64 values with a hot cache across seven input patterns (ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95, random_z1) on Zen 3; unstable contestants include rust_ipnsort_unstable (research-repo commit 757478b) and the pre-2024 Rust std sorts vendored mid 2022; MSVC rows are listed but not in the Linux plots.
corrections.caveats: Bias disclaimer: the ipnsort author wrote the analysis. Only 10k u64 on one CPU with 2023 toolchains (rustc 1.75 nightly, gcc 13.2.1, clang 16.0.6); the bitsetsort-derived libc++ std::sort of LLVM 17 is 'so far untested'. Driftsort (today's slice::sort) does not appear in this benchmark or in any C++ comparison found (the driftsort and ipnsort introductions compare only against Rust sorts), so the stable half of the record has no evidence against C++; the Rust stable sort shown (rust_std_stable, vendored mid 2022) is slower than libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random_d20 and random_p5 and slower than libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1. The ipnsort tested is the research-repo version at 757478b, not necessarily the code merged into std by rust-lang/rust PR 124032 (merged 2024-06-20). The win is algorithmic, not a Rust language effect: C++ pdqsort (144.4 us random) matches the pdqsort-based rust_std_unstable (136.9 us) and C crumsort (95.6 us) is close to ipnsort (77.0 us). ipnsort roughly ties libc++ on random_s95 (83.4 vs 84.2 us). Neither side uses -march=native for these contestants.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim, tier stays A for ipnsort: per-pattern numbers are readable on the plots (ipnsort 1.0x to 23.8x faster than libstdc++/libc++ std::sort), but driftsort is absent and the then-current Rust stable sort is slower than the C++ stable sorts on 2-3 of 7 patterns. Consider a name override to ipnsort (Rust std slice::sort_unstable) or a shortcoming saying driftsort has no C++ comparison. Metadata confirmed: 545 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-03-02 (active); rust-lang/rust PR 124032 merged 2024-06-20 replacing slice::sort with driftsort and sort_unstable with ipnsort.
